question: Can compositionality of an arbitrary representation be defined quantitatively as expressivity that is cheaply reconstructible from reusable discrete parts?

key_findings.claim: Representational compositionality is defined as a Kolmogorov-compression ratio, not merely reconstruction accuracy or distance preservation.
key_findings.evidence: The proposed C(Z)=K(Z)/K(Z|W) jointly optimizes a discrete sentence set W, its language prior, and a semantics program mapping sentences to representations. High scores require an expressive Z and a short semantics plus residual code; a language-system variant fixes externally supplied sentences.

key_findings.claim: Making the constituent vocabulary intrinsic via optimal compression is conceptually strong but renders the main metric uncomputable and non-identifiable in practice.
key_findings.evidence: C(Z) requires searching all languages, symbol sequences, and semantics programs. The paper sketches a discrete-autoencoder estimator but does not implement C(Z); actual real-data experiments use CL(Z), where sentences are already given, and replace Kolmogorov complexity with model-dependent prequential code lengths.

key_findings.claim: Controlled synthetic results align with several intuitions that topological similarity misses.
key_findings.evidence: For lookup-table representations, the score increases with sentence length, peaks at an intermediate vocabulary size, and decreases with embedding dimensionality and context dependence. For grammar-generated representations it decreases as rule width and depth increase; topological similarity gives contrary or noisier trends in several cases.

key_findings.claim: Prequential coding reproduces the expected ordering of emergent languages with and without iterated learning.
key_findings.evidence: In five-seed object-reference games, iterated-learning messages yield shorter codes for objects conditioned on messages and therefore higher CL(Z). The ordinary language reaches the minimum ratio near one, interpreted as an arbitrary map.

key_findings.claim: The natural-language comparison supports only a narrow statement about one translation-and-embedding pipeline, not language-intrinsic compositionality.
key_findings.evidence: COCO captions are machine-translated into five languages, their meanings are proxies from one multilingual sentence encoder, K(Z) is assumed equal, and only relative CL values are reported. Similar code lengths therefore may reflect the shared translation/encoder geometry; Japanese is slightly higher while topological similarity is anomalous.

method.core_idea: Call a representation compositional when it contains much information overall but can be losslessly described by short discrete sentences, a simple reusable semantics program, and small residual corrections.
method.mechanism: A hypothetical shortest program codes a sentence prior p(W), token sequences W, a semantics f that outputs distribution parameters for Z, and remaining reconstruction bits. C(Z) divides total representation complexity by the conditional complexity given optimal intrinsic sentences; CL(Z) fixes an external language. Synthetic cases use known generative programs, while real language systems estimate conditional complexity by sequentially training predictors and summing prequential predictive code lengths.
assumptions: Kolmogorov program length is the right abstraction for semantic simplicity despite dependence on a universal language up to additive constants.
Discrete token sequences are the appropriate constituent form for the representation being studied.
Practical compressors and neural predictors are tight, comparable upper bounds on the relevant complexities.
For cross-language comparison, representations are equally expressive and translation/embedding artifacts do not dominate.

techniques.role: Combines representational expressivity with simplicity of a parts-to-meaning map.
Defines constituents through the jointly optimal representation code rather than annotations.
Estimates conditional description length from online predictive performance.
Tests whether the metric follows controlled changes in grammar and lookup-table complexity.
Contrasts the complexity score with a common distance-correlation proxy.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic lookup-table and context-free-grammar representations with controlled sentence length, vocabulary, dimensionality, context dependence, rule width, and rule depth.
evaluations.result: C(Z) follows the authors' stated qualitative intuitions across all controlled factors and is less noisy than topological similarity on grammar draws.

evaluations.setting: Five-seed emergent object-reference languages trained normally or through iterated learning.
evaluations.metric: Prequential K(Z|W), CL(Z), and topological similarity.
evaluations.result: Iterated learning produces a shorter semantics code and a higher compositionality ratio, reproducing the established ordering.
evaluations.baseline: Normal multi-agent training without periodic generational resets.

evaluations.setting: COCO captions in English plus NLLB translations to French, Spanish, German, and Japanese, paired with multilingual sentence embeddings.
evaluations.metric: Three-seed prequential code length, relative CL(Z), and topological similarity.
evaluations.result: Relative scores cluster closely, with Japanese slightly higher; topological similarity places most languages near zero and Japanese below zero.
evaluations.baseline: Cross-language comparison under assumed equal K(Z).

limitations: The general intrinsic score C(Z) is uncomputable and is not estimated in the real-world experiments despite the abstract's tractability language.
Practical estimates can change with compressor, predictor architecture, hyperparameters, sample order, data quantity, precision, and universal-language constants.
A ratio can be difficult to compare when numerator and denominator estimates have different looseness or additive overheads.
The theory privileges discrete constituents and a Gaussian residual semantics; continuous or overlapping parts require extensions.
Synthetic experiments largely bake the preferred notion of simplicity into known generative programs.
The natural-language result is confounded by machine translation, image-caption genre, a shared multilingual encoder, and assumed equal expressivity.
failure_modes: A powerful decoder memorizes examples, yielding a deceptively short empirical code under favorable prequential choices.
Different tokenizations shift code between the language prior and semantics without representing a meaningful compositional change.
Low-dimensional or noisy representations appear simple because they are inexpressive rather than structurally compositional.
A compressor misses a compact latent grammar and substantially underestimates compositionality.
Cross-system score ordering reverses under a different precision, encoder, or predictor family.
reusable_insights: Evaluate compositional structure with both reconstruction and the complexity of the reconstructor; unconstrained decodability alone is insufficient.
Include expressivity in the numerator so trivial constant representations cannot maximize a compositionality score.
Use prequential coding as an operational complexity probe, but report sensitivity to model and coding choices.
Test structural metrics on factorized synthetic counterexamples before correlating them with downstream generalization.
Distinguish compositionality of a representation itself from compositionality relative to an externally supplied language.
open_questions: Can multiple independent compressors agree on stable rankings of intrinsic C(Z) for real neural representations?
How should continuous, probabilistic, hierarchical, or overlapping constituents enter the shortest-program definition?
Does estimated C(Z) predict compositional OOD generalization after controlling for representation dimension and task accuracy?
Can the score be optimized without decoder memorization or collapse to convenient tokenization artifacts?
How large are translation and multilingual-encoder effects in the reported cross-language ordering?

competitive_landscape.title: Measuring Compositionality in Representation Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Andreas measures how well a learned representation-producing model can be approximated by explicit inferred primitives. The present paper generalizes reconstruction scoring by charging for semantics complexity and making optimal constituents intrinsic, at the cost of uncomputability.

competitive_landscape.title: Linear Spaces of Meanings: Compositional Structures in Vision-Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Trager et al. test a concrete linear-subspace notion in VLM embeddings that is stable and actionable but restrictive. Complexity-based compositionality abstracts over nonlinear semantics and explicitly penalizes their program length.

competitive_landscape.title: What Makes Models Compositional? A Theoretical View
competitive_landscape.difference: Ram et al. define compositional functions and compositional complexity for sequence architectures, deriving expressivity and sample-complexity consequences. This paper instead scores arbitrary realized representations via optimal description length.

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding Simplicity Bias towards Compositional Mappings via Learning Dynamics
competitive_landscape.difference: Ren and Sutherland connect coding-length simplicity of compositional bijections to gradient-descent learning dynamics. The target paper turns the expressivity-versus-simplicity intuition into a representation-level ratio and broader empirical metric.

competitive_landscape.title: Improving Compositional Generalization using Iterated Learning and Simplicial Embeddings
competitive_landscape.difference: This NeurIPS 2023 work already motivates iterated learning through Kolmogorov-style compressibility and expressivity and demonstrates downstream gains. The target paper formalizes a general score rather than proposing a training method.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim a rigorous, quantitative, representation-agnostic definition that unifies expressivity, reusable symbolic parts, and simple semantics and can be estimated with deep-learning compression tools.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Sections 2-3 derive the program-length ratio; Section 5 validates controlled intuitions and applies the fixed-language form to emergent and natural languages.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The explicit ratio and intrinsic-parts optimal-code framing are a useful synthesis. Reconstruction metrics, linear composition, Kolmogorov simplicity arguments, and expressivity/compression accounts are direct predecessors. The largest gap is operational: the novel intrinsic quantity is never computed on real representations, so current evidence validates a fixed-language surrogate.

reviewer_notes: Read all 32 cached pages, including estimator, synthetic derivations, prequential protocol, natural-language caveats, and appendices. Direct primary-source competitors from arXiv/OpenReview were checked on 2026-08-23. Claims are calibrated to distinguish the uncomputed intrinsic score C(Z) from the experimentally estimated language-relative CL(Z).
